summary.text: A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy of about 1,000 up to several billion stars, compared with the Milky Way's 100 to 400 billion.
Their formation and activity are thought to be heavily influenced by interactions with larger galaxies, and some have been seen pulled apart by neighbouring spirals.
Many dwarf galaxies in the Local Group orbit larger galaxies, and more than 20 known dwarfs orbit the Milky Way.

paragraphs.heading: Small galaxies
paragraphs.text: A dwarf galaxy is a small galaxy, holding anywhere from about 1,000 to several billion stars. For comparison, the Milky Way has 100 to 400 billion. The line is not always sharp: the Large Magellanic Cloud, which orbits close to the Milky Way and has more than 30 billion stars, is called a dwarf by some and a full galaxy by others. Astronomers sort dwarfs into many types by their shape and makeup.

paragraphs.heading: Living near giants
paragraphs.text: The way dwarf galaxies form and behave is thought to depend heavily on their dealings with bigger galaxies. Our Local Group has many of them, and they often orbit larger galaxies such as the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum. More than 20 known dwarfs circle the Milky Way. Because they are small, some have been seen pulled toward a neighbouring spiral and torn apart, leaving streams of stars and in the end merging with it. Omega Centauri, the Milky Way's largest globular cluster, may in fact be what is left of a dwarf galaxy's core, which has a central black hole and which our galaxy took in at some point.

paragraphs.heading: Where dwarfs come from
paragraphs.text: One theory holds that most galaxies, dwarfs included, form along with dark matter or from gas that contains metals. Yet NASA's Galaxy Evolution Explorer found new dwarfs forming from gas low in metals, inside the Leo Ring, a hydrogen and helium cloud surrounding two massive galaxies in the constellation Leo. Tidal dwarf galaxies form when galaxies collide: their gravity drags streams of material away from the parent galaxies and the dark matter halos around them. A 2007 paper suggested that galactic tides during the early growth of the Milky Way and Andromeda created many dwarfs. A 2018 study suggests some local dwarfs formed within the first billion years after the Big Bang.

paragraphs.heading: Some notable kinds
paragraphs.text: Blue compact dwarfs hold large clusters of young, hot, massive stars, and the brightest of these are blue, which makes the whole galaxy look blue. Ultra-faint dwarfs hold only a few hundred to a hundred thousand stars, which makes them the faintest galaxies in the Universe. They look like globular clusters but are more spread out and carry a lot of dark matter; in fact they are the most dark-matter-dominated systems known. They were first found in 2005 with digital sky surveys, in particular the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. At the other extreme, ultra-compact dwarfs are thought to pack about 100 million stars into a space roughly 200 light years across.

paragraphs.heading: Why astronomers study them
paragraphs.text: Small as they are, dwarfs are useful. Tracking how single stars move in nearby dwarfs, such as the Sculptor Dwarf Galaxy, lets scientists test what the standard cosmological model predicts. Close studies also show how surroundings, for example ram pressure stripping, shape the way galaxies form and change. All the ultra-faint dwarfs found so far are ancient, likely formed only a few million years after the Big Bang, so they may hold clues about the early Universe. And surveys such as the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program find that 30–50% of dwarfs in low-density surroundings are quenched, meaning they form few new stars.
